The Aurora Borealis, also known as the Northern Lights, is caused by the interaction between the Earth's magnetic field and charged particles from the sun. These particles, primarily electrons and protons, emanate from the solar wind, which is a stream of charged particles released from the sun's corona.

When the solar wind reaches Earth, it can disturb the outer part of the Earth's magnetic field, known as the magnetosphere. Some of these charged particles become trapped in the Earth's magnetic field and are funneled towards the polar regions. As they travel through the magnetosphere and into the upper atmosphere (about 80 to 300 kilometers above the Earth), they collide with gas molecules, such as nitrogen and oxygen. These collisions transfer energy to the gas molecules, which then release this energy as light to return to their original state, creating the beautiful colors observed in the auroras.

The specific colors of the Aurora Borealis depend on the type of gas involved and the altitude of the interaction. Oxygen at high altitudes (above 150 kilometers) can emit a red color, while at lower altitudes (around 95 to 120 kilometers), it tends to emit a green color, which is most common. Nitrogen can produce purples, blues, or pink colors, depending on the type of nitrogen molecule and its state.

The intensity and frequency of auroral displays are also influenced by solar activity, such as solar flares or coronal mass ejections, which can increase the number of particles in the solar wind, leading to more vivid and widespread auroras.
